lead: Angular is a TypeScript framework for single-page apps, and its unit of work is the component: a class that holds data and behaviour, plus an HTML template that displays it, joined by a decorator. Bindings keep the two sides in step. Read this chapter and you can open any Angular component file and say which decorator makes it a component, how {{ }} and [ ] push values into the page, how ( ) and [( )] bring clicks and typing back, and how directives and pipes reshape markup without extra class code.
prereq: You need: 5.5 for classes, interfaces and decorators, and Unit 2 for HTML attributes, CSS classes and styles.

sections.h3: A class plus a template, joined by a decorator

blocks.text: A component is a TypeScript class plus an HTML template. The class alone shows nothing on screen. A decorator joins the two.

@Component is that decorator. Its object has four common keys. selector is the CSS tag the component answers to, such as app-product-card. templateUrl points to the HTML file. styleUrls lists CSS files whose rules apply only inside this template. imports lists what the template needs, such as FormsModule or another component.

The CLI puts components in src/app; main.ts starts the app and angular.json describes the build. Older Angular (2 to 14) declared every component in an @NgModule declarations array. Newer Angular marks the component standalone: true and imports it directly. Some syllabi call the first module-based and the second standalone; both appear on question papers.

AngularJS is not Angular. AngularJS means version 1.x: plain JavaScript, ng-app, ng-controller, and a $scope object shared with the view. Angular means version 2 and later: a rewrite in TypeScript built on components. An answer about $scope in an Angular 2+ question scores nothing.
Data binding is how the class and the template exchange values. The direction of the arrow is the thing to remember.

Property binding sets a DOM property, not an HTML attribute. [disabled]="flag" works because a button has a boolean disabled property. When the DOM property name differs from the attribute name, use attr. binding, for example [attr.aria-label]="label". Class and style binding switch one class or one style at a time; ngClass and ngStyle handle many.
Event binding calls a class method. (click)="save()" passes nothing; (input)="onType($event)" passes the browser event, where $event.target.value is the typed text.

Two-way binding writes in both directions. [(ngModel)]="qty" is short for [ngModel]="qty" plus (ngModelChange)="qty=$event". It needs FormsModule in the component's imports array, or in the NgModule's imports. Without that import the template does not compile: Angular reports that ngModel is not a known property of input (NG8002). Only schemas: [NO_ERRORS_SCHEMA], which is not recommended, would let the box accept typing with no effect on the class field.
A directive changes DOM that already exists in the template, or decides whether it exists at all. Two kinds matter.

Structural directives add or remove elements, so they carry a leading *. *ngIf="ok" keeps the element only while ok is true. For an else branch, name a template: *ngIf="ok; else loading" with <ng-template #loading>…</ng-template>. *ngFor="let p of products; index as i" repeats the element once per item. Add trackBy: byId with a method byId(i, p) { return p.id; } so Angular moves existing rows instead of rebuilding the list. [ngSwitch]="status" with *ngSwitchCase and *ngSwitchDefault picks one block from many.

Attribute directives restyle or rewire an element that stays in place: ngClass, ngStyle, ngModel. Write your own with @Directive({selector: '[appHighlight]'}) and a @HostListener('mouseenter') method that runs when the mouse enters the host element.

A pipe reshapes a value for display only; the class field is unchanged. {{ price | currency:'INR' }} prints ₹2,499.00, {{ name | uppercase }} prints FILTER COFFEE, and {{ today | date:'dd/MM/yyyy' }} prints the date in that pattern. Leave out the currency code and the pipe falls back to dollars.

@Input() product marks a field the parent fills: <app-product-card [product]="p">. @Output() add = new EventEmitter<Product>() marks a field that fires events upward; the parent listens with (add)="onAdd($event)", and add.emit(product) puts product into $event.

Lifecycle hooks run at fixed moments. ngOnChanges runs before ngOnInit and again on every input change. ngOnInit runs once, after the first inputs arrive, which is where you load data. ngOnDestroy runs just before removal, where you stop timers and unsubscribe. This is the same idea as mounting and unmounting in 5.2.

Angular Material gives ready-made Material Design widgets such as toolbar, table, dialog and snackbar. Older projects use Flex-Layout attributes like fxLayout="row" and fxFlex; that package is deprecated, so newer code writes the same layout in plain CSS with flexbox or grid.

figure.caption: The class pushes values into the template and the DOM with {{ }} and [ ]; clicks and typing travel back up with ( ) and [(ngModel)].

spec.title: Component, template, DOM
spec.aria: A component class feeds a template using interpolation and property binding, the template renders the DOM, and event binding and two-way binding send changes back from the template to the class.

examples.question:
A ProductCard component has the field product = {id: 3, name: 'Filter coffee', price: 2499}, where price is in rupees. Its template contains these lines:

{{ product.name | uppercase }}

{{ product.price | currency:'INR' }}

Total: {{ product.price * qty | currency:'INR' }}

The user types 3 into the input. State exactly what the card displays on each line, and what reaches the parent's (add) handler when the button is clicked.
steps: The class holds name = 'Filter coffee' and price = 2499 rupees. Nothing is displayed yet; Angular reads these when it renders the template.
{{ product.name | uppercase }} passes the string through the uppercase pipe: 'Filter coffee' becomes 'FILTER COFFEE'.

{{ product.price | currency:'INR' }} formats the number in the app's current locale, by default en-US: comma every three digits, dot as decimal. The pipe takes only the currency code INR from the argument, so the symbol is ₹ and there are two decimals: ₹2,499.00. Registering the en-IN locale would change large values to lakh/crore grouping, such as ₹2,49,900.00.

Typing 3 into <input type="number" [(ngModel)]="qty"> writes the number 3 into the class field qty. This works only because FormsModule is imported; without it the template fails to compile with the ngModel-not-a-known-property error. A plain text input would write the string "3": multiplication still works by number coercion, but adding it to price would concatenate strings.
The total expression is product.price × qty = 2499 × 3 = 7497 rupees, shown as ₹7,497.00, so the paragraph reads: Total: ₹7,497.00.

The click runs add.emit(product). The EventEmitter carries the object {id: 3, name: 'Filter coffee', price: 2499}, which arrives as $event in the parent's (add)="onAdd($event)" handler. qty is not sent, because only product is passed to emit.
examples.answer: The card shows FILTER COFFEE, ₹2,499.00 and Total: ₹7,497.00, and the click sends {id: 3, name: 'Filter coffee', price: 2499} up to the parent as $event.
examples.check:
price = 2499
qty = 3
total = price * qty
print(f"{price:.2f}")
print(f"{total:.2f}")

traps: AngularJS answers in an Angular 2+ question: ng-app, ng-controller and $scope belong to version 1.x, a different framework written in JavaScript. They score zero here.

Property versus attribute: colspan is an attribute whose DOM property is spelled colSpan. Property binding matches names exactly, so [colspan] finds nothing and fails, while [colSpan]="cols" and the always-safe [attr.colspan]="cols" both work. Use attr. binding for attribute-only names such as aria-label.
Leaving out the star: ngIf and ngFor without * bind nothing; they are only structural with the asterisk. The examiner looks for the * first.
Without FormsModule the template does not compile: Angular throws 'Can't bind to ngModel since it isn't a known property of input' (NG8002). The page breaks; it does not silently show blanks.

Without trackBy, Angular matches rows by object identity. A new array of new objects makes it throw away and rebuild every row, losing input focus and animations. A trackBy returning a stable id (p.id, not the index) lets Angular move existing rows.

quiz.q: What does the selector key inside @Component do?
quiz.a: It gives the CSS tag the component answers to, for example app-product-card, which the parent template then uses as an element.

quiz.q: Which module must be imported for [(ngModel)] to work?
quiz.a: FormsModule, listed in the component's imports (or the NgModule's imports).

quiz.q: Why is [disabled]="flag" reliable while disabled="{{flag}}" is not?
quiz.a: Property binding assigns the real boolean DOM property, so true and false both behave. Interpolation writes the string "true" or "false" into the attribute, and any non-empty string disables the button.

quiz.q: A template lists 100 products with *ngFor. Write the two pieces needed so that only changed rows are touched, and say what the method returns.
quiz.a: In the template: *ngFor="let p of products; trackBy: byId". In the class: byId(index: number, p: Product) { return p.id; }. It returns the stable id of the product.

quiz.q: Give the exact text printed by {{ 2499 | currency:'INR' }} and by {{ 'filter coffee' | uppercase }}.
quiz.a: ₹2,499.00 and FILTER COFFEE. The currency pipe adds the rupee symbol, thousands grouping and two decimal places.

quiz.q: A parent changes [product] on an existing child component. ngOnChanges fires but ngOnInit does not. Explain why, and say where the child should react to the new value.
quiz.a: ngOnInit runs exactly once, after the first set of inputs. Later input changes only raise ngOnChanges, which receives a SimpleChanges map of old and new values; reacting to new data belongs there (or in a setter), not in ngOnInit.

quiz.q: A student writes (click)="save" instead of (click)="save()". What happens and why?
quiz.a: The text inside ( ) is evaluated as a statement. "save" is just a property read that returns the method reference; Angular ignores that value and never calls it, so the click does nothing and no error appears. (click)="save()" calls it with no arguments, and (click)="save($event)" or (click)="save(item)" passes the event or a value explicitly.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer Angular adds signals: a value wrapped so the template re-renders only where that value is read, which is finer-grained than checking the whole component tree. Standalone components have become the default shape of a project, so the NgModule pattern is mostly seen in older code. Change detection without Zone.js is being rolled out, and @defer blocks let a template load a heavy part only when it scrolls into view. Search for Angular signals, standalone components and zoneless change detection to follow this.
